title: Store an enum by name, not by ordinal

blocks.text: The page warns that `ordinal()` is a fragile thing to persist: add or reorder a constant and every stored number points at a different constant. Persist the `name()` instead. It also recommends a `safeValueOf` that wraps `Enum.valueOf` in an `Optional`, because `valueOf` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for an unknown name and `NullPointerException` for `null`.
The starter has two releases of one enum: `StatusV1 { ACTIVE, INACTIVE }` and the later `StatusV2 { PENDING, ACTIVE, INACTIVE }`, which added `PENDING` in front. Write:

items: `static String store(Enum<?> constant)`: the text to persist for `constant`.

`static <E extends Enum<E>> Optional<E> load(Class<E> type, String stored)`: the constant of `type` that `stored` names, or an empty `Optional` when `stored` is `null` or names no constant. The match is exact: case and spaces count.

blocks.text: The stored text comes back from a database or a file, so it is a fresh `String` object, never the constant's own name object.

cases.says: What store() writes for a constant, load() reads back as the same constant.
A value stored by the old enum loads as the same-named constant of a newer enum that added a constant in front.
A stored text that was built at run time, not written as a literal, still finds its constant.
A stored text that names no constant exactly (another case, extra spaces, an unknown name) loads as an empty Optional instead of throwing.
A null stored text loads as an empty Optional instead of throwing.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: An enum is persisted by name() or a stable code, because stored ordinals point at different constants once constants are added or reordered.
Enum.valueOf throws for an unknown name and for null, so a safe lookup wraps it and returns an Optional.
